common_name: Blackberry Frost Hens and Chicks (Chick Charms Series Deep Purple Sempervivum)

planting.note: Press offsets onto the surface of lean, gritty, sharply drained soil in full sun; deepest purple color develops with strong light and cool nights.

directions: A member of the Chick Charms breeding series, 'Blackberry Frost' carries tightly cupped leaves in a deep aubergine-purple that darkens toward black at the tips in cold weather, with a faint silvery bloom giving the rosette a frosted look. Full sun and lean, mineral soil bring out the richest color, while shade or overly rich soil produces looser, greener rosettes that lose the frosted sheen. Water only after the gritty mix has dried completely, since this compact selection rots quickly if kept damp through winter. It offsets readily on short stolons to form a dense mat, making it well suited to troughs, crevice gardens, and rock garden edges.

common_name: Cranapple Hens and Chicks (Chick Charms Series Red-and-Green Sempervivum)

planting.note: Press offsets onto the surface of lean, sharply drained gravelly soil in full sun in spring or fall.

directions: 'Cranapple' is a Chick Charms selection whose open rosette shifts between apple-green leaf centers and a cranberry-red outer band, the contrast sharpening as nights cool in spring and fall. Plant offsets directly on the surface of gritty, fast-draining soil in full sun, since bright light is what drives the strongest two-tone color; in shade the rosette stays largely green. It multiplies steadily by short-stemmed offsets to form a spreading colony within a couple of seasons, and needs no winter protection where drainage is sharp, as excess moisture around the crown is a greater threat than cold.

common_name: Damask Rose Hens and Chicks (Chick Charms Series Dusky Pink Sempervivum)

planting.note: Press offsets onto the surface of lean, gritty, sharply drained soil in full sun; dusky rose tones deepen with cooler temperatures.

directions: 'Damask Rose' bears rounded, closely overlapping leaves in a soft dusky pink that flushes deeper mauve-rose through the cool seasons and softens toward gray-green in summer heat. Grow in lean, mineral soil with sharp drainage and full sun, setting offsets on the soil surface rather than burying the crown, and let the mix dry fully between waterings. Like other sempervivums it flowers only once per rosette on a tall stalk before that rosette dies, but the surrounding chicks continue the clump indefinitely. It is fully winter hardy and tolerates snow cover without protection, making it a dependable choice for troughs and rock gardens.

common_name: Grape Tart Hens and Chicks (Chick Charms Series Purple-Violet Sempervivum)

planting.note: Press offsets onto the surface of lean, sharply drained gravelly soil in full sun in spring or fall.

directions: Named for its rich violet-purple coloring, 'Grape Tart' forms a tight, globular rosette of pointed leaves that hold their grape-toned color through most of the growing season and deepen further with cold. Full sun and lean, sharply drained soil bring out the strongest pigment; plants grown in shade or damp, fertile soil turn duller and greener. It stays compact, offsetting into a slowly spreading mat that suits small containers, troughs, and tight crevices between paving stones. Water sparingly and avoid overhead irrigation that leaves water sitting in the rosette, which encourages rot.

common_name: Sugar Baby Hens and Chicks (Chick Charms Series Compact Pink-Tipped Sempervivum)

planting.note: Press small offsets onto the surface of lean, gritty, sharply drained soil in full sun; keep this miniature selection from being crowded by larger neighbors.

directions: 'Sugar Baby' is one of the smallest Chick Charms selections, forming a diminutive pale green rosette barely an inch or two across with soft pink tips that brighten in cool weather. Its small scale makes it easy to lose among more vigorous hens and chicks, so it does best planted where larger neighbors will not crowd it, in lean, gritty, sharply drained soil in full sun. It offsets readily on very short stolons, filling in a shallow trough or miniature container over a season or two. Keep it on the dry side, as its small rosette size leaves little buffer against rot from standing moisture.

common_name: Wine and Roses Hens and Chicks (Chick Charms Series Wine-Red Sempervivum)

planting.note: Press offsets onto the surface of lean, sharply drained gravelly soil in full sun in spring or fall.

directions: 'Wine and Roses' produces medium rosettes in a deep wine-red that intensifies to near-burgundy through fall and winter, softening to a rosier tone during the height of the growing season. Grow in lean, mineral, sharply drained soil in full sun, where strong light sustains the darkest color; plants sited in shade fade toward plain green. Offsets form steadily on short stolons, building a dense colony that works well massed in a rock garden border or mixed succulent trough. As with other sempervivums, avoid soil that stays wet, since this is a far greater risk to the plant than winter cold.

common_name: Phyllis Hutchinson Aeonium (Green-and-Red Flat Rosette Aeonium)

planting.note: Grow as a houseplant or xeriscape container plant in bright light to full sun in fast-draining, gritty succulent mix; red leaf margins deepen in bright, cool-season light.

directions: 'Phyllis Hutchinson' forms a low, flattened rosette of rounded green leaves edged in a thin band of red that intensifies with bright light and cool temperatures, giving the clump a two-tone rim effect distinct from the fully tricolor aeonium cultivars. Grow in bright light to full sun in fast-draining, gritty succulent mix, providing afternoon shade only in the hottest inland climates. Offsets form at the base to build a slowly spreading clump of rosettes over time, and like other aeoniums it grows most actively through the cooler months, slowing or going semi-dormant in summer heat. Propagate easily from stem or rosette cuttings allowed to callus for several days before setting into dry mix.

common_name: Oblong-Leaf Pig's Ear (Narrow-Leaf Cotyledon orbiculata Variety)

planting.note: Root leaf or stem cuttings after callusing for several days, then plant into gritty, fast-draining succulent mix in bright light once frost danger has passed.

directions: Var. oblonga is a naturally occurring form of pig's ear distinguished from the typical rounded-leaf species by its longer, narrower, tongue-shaped leaves, still coated in the same powdery gray-white bloom. Grow in bright light to full sun in fast-draining, gritty succulent mix, watering deeply only once the soil has dried, since the waxy coating that protects the leaves rubs off easily with handling and heavy moisture invites rot. It develops into a small, sparsely branched shrublet over several years, eventually sending up tall stalks of orange-red bell flowers above the foliage. In frost-free climates it suits a xeriscape bed, while colder gardens should grow it in a container that can be moved under cover for winter.
sources: Cactus and Succulent Society of America reference
